objection: Does ‘firstborn of creation’ mean Jesus was created?
answer: I really appreciate you wrestling honestly with this rather than just accepting a slogan—that's exactly the right instinct, because the word does look like it settles the matter at first glance. But "firstborn" (Greek *prototokos*) in Scripture is regularly a title of rank and inheritance, not birth order. Psalm 89:27 calls David God's "firstborn" even though David was the youngest of Jesse's sons, not God's first or only child in any literal sense—clearly a statement about status, not origin. Paul removes any doubt in the very next verse: "For by him were all things created, that are in heaven, and that are in earth, visible and invisible, whether they be thrones, or dominions, or principalities, or powers: all things were created by him, and for him" (Colossians 1:16). If Christ is the one *through whom* "all things" were created, he cannot himself be one of the created things—that would be incoherent, him creating himself. So Paul's own logic places the Son on the Creator side of the line, not as the first creature but as the one who holds the position of preeminence and heir over all creation, precisely because "in him all things hold together." You're not dodging the plain meaning by reading it this way—you're following Paul's own argument to where he explicitly takes it.

# Objection: "Firstborn of Creation"

I've been reading Colossians 1:15, where it says Jesus is "the firstborn of all creation," and I keep getting stuck on it. I *want* to believe he's God and eternal, but doesn't "firstborn" kind of... mean he was born? Like, if he's the *first* thing created, doesn't that make him created—just before everything else? I've seen people make this point, and honestly, I don't know how to answer them without feeling like I'm dodging the plain meaning of the words.

That's such a fair question to sit with—you're taking the text seriously rather than rushing past it, and that's exactly the right instinct. The good news is that the very next verse in Colossians answers it, so you're not being asked to dodge anything; you're being asked to keep reading.

Start with what "firstborn" (prototokos) actually meant in that world. It wasn't primarily a birth-order word; it was a rank-and-inheritance word. Psalm 89:27 calls David God's "firstborn," even though David was the youngest son in his family and not remotely God's first created being. "Firstborn" designates preeminence and heirship—the one who holds the place of highest honor—not "the first one made."

Then look at how Paul himself immediately unpacks it. Colossians 1:16 says, "For by him were all things created, that are in heaven, and that are in earth, visible and invisible... all things were created by him, and for him." If Christ is the *agent* through whom "all things" came to be, he cannot simultaneously be one of the "all things" that came to be—that would be self-contradictory, like saying the carpenter is also one of the chairs he built. Paul places him on the Creator side of the line, not the creature side.

John says the same thing with total clarity: "All things were made by him; and without him was not any thing made that was made" (John 1:3). "Without exception" leaves no room for Christ himself to be an exception.

So "firstborn of all creation" means: the one who has supreme rank *over* creation, the heir of all things, the one for whom and by whom it exists—not the first item on creation's list. You're not dodging the plain meaning; you're letting Paul's own next sentence define his own first sentence, which is the most honest way to read anyone.

If Christ is the one *through whom* "all things" were created, he cannot himself be one of the created things—that would be incoherent, him creating himself. So Paul's own logic places the Son on the Creator side of the line, not as the first creature but as the one who holds the position of preeminence and heir over all creation, precisely because "in him all things hold together." You're not dodging the plain meaning by reading it this way—you're following Paul's own argument to where he explicitly takes it.
